blockingProblems: The chapter's entire payload is a critique of a published research protocol, and it cites not one instance of that protocol. Line 103 announces 'The protocol at issue is the supervised one, and I state it in full because the objection that follows is aimed at the procedure rather than at anyone's implementation of it' — then describes a Monte-Carlo-sample, label, classify, crossing-at-one-half pipeline that is recognisably a specific published method, with zero citation. 'Carrasquilla', 'Melko', 'van Nieuwenburg' and every other machine-learning name appear zero times in the file. A university press referee will not accept a chapter that attacks a literature without naming a single member of it. The disclaimer that the objection targets 'the procedure rather than anyone's implementation' is a rhetorical dodge, not scholarly apparatus. Note also that the ch01 packet supplies no ML verifiedClaims at all, so the author had no sourced basis for characterising the protocol and proceeded regardless.

The technical core is unattributed while the historical narrative is scrupulously credited, and the asymmetry is indefensible. The section 'No singularity fits in a finite box' (lines 79-99) is built entirely on partition-function zeros — 'in the variable x = e^{-beta epsilon} ... Z_N is a polynomial ... two arcs of roots pinch the real axis' (lines 85-89) — which is Yang-Lee and Fisher zero theory. The chapter names nobody, gives no eponym and offers no citation, so a reader who wants to follow it up has no search term; 'Lee' appears zero times in the file. The same holds for finite-size scaling (lines 93-97), for hyperscaling '2 - alpha = d nu' (line 67), and for the upper critical dimension. Meanwhile Peierls gets a year, a venue and a DOI for a one-clause mention. A Cambridge or Princeton monograph does not credit the 1936 anecdote and silently appropriate the 1952 machinery.

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is derived in full (lines 23-25) and never named. The chapter works through 'Per particle, d mu = -s dT + v dp' to 'dp/dT = Delta S / Delta V = L/(T Delta V)' and closes on the kettle carried up a mountain without once telling the reader what the result is called; 'Clausius' and 'Clapeyron' each appear zero times. A graduate student finishes that passage unable to look it up. Same defect as the zeros section: the book teaches the physics and withholds the vocabulary.

Structural failure in the middle third. The chronology runs 1937 (Landau, line 43), 1972 (Wilson-Fisher, line 61), 1945 (Guggenheim, 63), 1925 (Ising, 65), 1936 (Peierls), 1944 (Onsager), 1952 (Yang), 1965 (Widom, 67), 1963 (Rushbrooke), 1966 (Kadanoff, 69), 1971 (Wilson), 1974 (Fisher). The reader is handed the resolution of the mean-field crisis before being shown the crisis. Line 61 is a single orphaned sentence naming the epsilon expansion that explains nothing: it asserts 'a controlled perturbative series about the upper critical dimension four' and that 'setting epsilon = 1 yields usable three-dimensional values' without saying what a non-integer dimension means or why a series evaluated at epsilon = 1 should be trusted. That is a name-drop, not exposition.

The renormalisation group, the actual answer to the question the chapter poses, is compressed into three sentences (line 69) asserting 'critical points as fixed points and exponents as eigenvalues of the linearized flow' with no account of how an eigenvalue becomes an exponent and no mention of relevant and irrelevant operators. Compare the 300-word treatment of the Ginzburg criterion at line 59. The chapter spends its rigor on the diagnosis and skimps on the cure, then makes universality load-bearing at line 69 ('the hinge on which the last section of this chapter turns') when the last section invokes universality exactly once, in a subordinate clause at line 117. The forward reference is never paid off.
styleViolations: Cadence tic: nearly every section terminates on the same short antithetical clincher, and by the fourth instance it is predictable. Line 5 'Between the two phases there is nothing.' Line 19 'The envelope is continuous; its gradient is not.' Line 65 'One eighth is not one half, and a logarithmic divergence is not a finite jump.' Line 75 'Not a jump. A divergence.' Line 83 'A finite system has no phase transition whatsoever.' Line 97 'Larger systems have narrower crossovers. No system has a singularity.' Line 115 'the number being reported describes an object present in neither.' Eleven section- and paragraph-ends execute the identical rhetorical move. It reads as a generation habit, not a voice.

The 'not X. It is Y.' construction recurs at least seven times: line 7 'That is not a technicality. It is why the subject is hard'; line 21 'Analyticity is not lost by any single phase. It is lost by the operation of taking a minimum over phases'; line 59 'Four is not a round number chosen for convenience. It is where that exponent changes sign.'; line 91 'The singularity is therefore not absent ... It is present as'; line 99 'The infinite-system answer is not read off the data. It is imported as an ansatz'; line 107 'The quantity plotted against temperature is not the network. It is the average'; line 119 'the useful response is not to check the number against Onsager ... It is to ask'. At book length this is a tell.

Line 105 spends a full paragraph erecting an argument the author then declines to make: 'The natural first move is to argue from the function class, observing that the standard smooth activations are real-analytic ... That move is unavailable here.' Roughly a hundred words of setup to knock down a position nobody has taken. The point survives at a third the length.

Throat-clearing and defensive first person at line 103: 'and I state it in full because the objection that follows is aimed at the procedure rather than at anyone's implementation of it, including the implementation this book builds.' Two pre-emptive apologies before the argument starts. Line 117's 'My expectation is that the second dominates' followed by 'The expectation is testable' reads as a grant abstract rather than a monograph.

The ending does not escalate. Line 117 has already laid out the experiment ('Hold the protocol fixed, vary L, and see whether the crossing drifts at the rate the correlation length dictates'), so line 119's closing 'and then to build the experiment that would say' restates rather than advances, and 'the experiment that would say' is clipped to the point of sounding unfinished. The packet's open question, what a network is actually detecting, lands with markedly less force than the opening kettle.

Copyediting: the same two people are introduced twice in two different name forms. Line 61 has 'Kenneth G. Wilson and Michael E. Fisher'; line 69 then re-introduces both at full length as 'Kenneth Geddes Wilson' and 'Michael Ellis Fisher'. Standard practice is full name at first mention, surname thereafter. A press copyeditor catches this on the first pass.

Apparatus: 'Citations used in this chapter' (line 121) is not monograph apparatus; presses use notes or a bibliography. The body prose carries no note markers at all, so no individual assertion is tied to any individual source, which is what allows the unattributed zeros and finite-size-scaling material to pass unnoticed.
factProblems: 'the Ginzburg criterion' (line 59) is an eponymous attribution to a named person, Vitaly Ginzburg, who appears nowhere in the packet's verifiedClaims. No paper, year or venue is given. The chapter's most detailed single technical argument therefore rests on an attribution with no ground truth behind it. Either source it or state the criterion without the name.

Line 57: 'Landau's expansion carries an assumption that took thirty years to interpret correctly.' Unsourced quantitative historical claim with no packet support, and it does not survive arithmetic. From Landau 1937 the Ginzburg criterion is about twenty-three years later, Kadanoff twenty-nine, Wilson thirty-four. 'Thirty years' is a rounded gesture presented as fact.

Line 61 gives Wilson and Fisher no year in the body, while every other figure carries one in-text (1933, 1937, 1925, 1936, 1944, 1952, 1945, 1965, 1963, 1966, 1971, 1974). The packet fixes it at 1972 and the reference list has it; the body silently omits it, around the one paper whose date matters most to the chapter's scrambled chronology.

Reference line 124 attaches https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03062 to the Ehrenfest 1933 entry with no note that it resolves to Sauer's 2016 preprint of the translation rather than to Ehrenfest's paper. The packet's own correction flags this locator explicitly and instructs that it be labelled as Sauer's preprint. The correction was applied to the Sauer line (125) but not to the Ehrenfest line, so a reader following the Ehrenfest citation lands on an unlabelled 2016 posting by a different author.

Line 61 states that mean-field theory is exact at d = 4 'up to multiplicative logarithmic corrections.' The physics is right, but the packet says only 'where mean-field theory becomes exact'; the qualifier is an unsourced embellishment. Harmless alone, symptomatic of a chapter that adds unsourced technical detail wherever it feels confident.

Verified clean, for the record. Mechanical style scan over all 137 lines: zero em dashes, zero en dashes, zero occurrences of '--', zero bullet or numbered lists, no summary or recap section. All five packet corrections that bear on this chapter were applied: Sauer is dated 2017 with EPJ Special Topics 226, 539-549 (lines 33 and 125), and Rushbrooke's 1963 inequality is correctly placed as preceding Widom 1965 (lines 67 and 132); the Berezinskii, 2021 Nobel and Turnbull-Fisher corrections concern material this chapter does not use. Numbers check out: latent heat over specific heat is about 539, so 'several hundred times' (line 3) is right; the liquid-vapour density ratio at 1 atm is about 1600, so 'about three orders of magnitude' (line 5) is right. The Landau minimum (line 51), the Ginzburg ratio exponent (d-4)/2 (line 59), hyperscaling giving nu = 1 in two dimensions (line 67), the log-L specific-heat peak (line 97) and the analyticity of the Boltzmann average of f_theta (line 111) are all correct. Every named person, year and venue except Ginzburg traces to the packet.
whatWouldMakeItAAA: Three fixes, in order of severity. First, cite the target. The chapter cannot critique a supervised protocol at book length while naming no paper that uses it; obtain the ML citations the packet failed to supply, name the specific studies, quote their reported critical temperatures, so the objection at line 119 lands on real work rather than a composite the author assembled. Second, close the attribution gap in the technical core: name Yang and Lee, and Fisher for the complex-temperature zeros the chapter actually uses at line 85, in the finite-box section; name the Clausius-Clapeyron relation at line 25; name Josephson at the hyperscaling step; source the Ginzburg criterion. As it stands the chapter credits the anecdotes and quietly borrows the machinery. Third, rebuild the middle. Move the Wilson-Fisher paragraph (line 61) to after Kadanoff and Wilson so the chronology runs crisis then resolution, and either expand the RG paragraph at line 69 to earn the weight the chapter places on universality or stop calling universality 'the hinge on which the last section turns' when that section barely touches it. Then, at sentence level, break the cadence: strike half the clipped antitheses that close each section, cut the 'not X. It is Y.' construction to two appearances, delete the defensive clauses at line 103, compress the declined function-class argument at line 105 to one sentence, and give the final paragraph something the preceding one has not already said. The opening three paragraphs are genuinely first-rate and would survive any blind comparison; the chapter's problem is that little after line 59 is written or sourced to that standard.
